concepts.name: Origins and Trigger of the Swadeshi Movement: Partition of Bengal (1905)
key_dimensions: Administrative vs. political motives behind Lord Curzon's partition decision
The announced date (July 19, 1905) vs. implementation date (October 16, 1905) and their significance
Role of 'divide and rule' policy along religious lines (Muslim-majority East Bengal vs. Hindu-majority West Bengal)
How partition acted as the immediate catalyst distinguishing Swadeshi from earlier economic nationalism

concepts.name: Rakhi Bandhan and the 'Day of Mourning' — Symbolic Politics of Swadeshi
key_dimensions: Rabindranath Tagore's role in organizing mass tying of rakhis on October 16, 1905 as a symbol of Hindu-Muslim unity
Arandhan (non-lighting of hearths) as a form of passive resistance
Distinction between symbolic protest and active political agitation within the movement
UPSC trap: Tagore later became a critic of certain strands of nationalism — linking his Swadeshi participation to his later critiques

concepts.name: Economic Dimensions of Swadeshi: Boycott of British Goods
key_dimensions: Distinction between Swadeshi (use of indigenous goods) and Boycott (refusal of foreign goods) as two separate but linked strategies
Impact on Manchester textile industry and Lancashire mills — British economic anxiety
Limits of boycott: inability to sustain without alternative indigenous industries
Comparison with later Gandhian constructive programme — continuities and departures

concepts.name: Ideological Factions within the Swadeshi Movement: Moderates vs. Extremists
key_dimensions: Moderate position (Gopal Krishna Gokhale): Swadeshi as economic self-reliance, opposition to mass agitation and boycott of councils
Extremist position (Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lala Lajpat Rai — Lal-Bal-Pal): Swadeshi as political weapon for Swaraj
Aurobindo Ghose's position — passive resistance as a middle path with revolutionary undertones
UPSC trap: Gokhale supported Swadeshi as an idea but opposed its extension into political boycott — nuance often tested

concepts.name: The Surat Split (1907): Organizational Consequence of the Swadeshi Era
key_dimensions: Immediate cause: disagreement over presidency of the Congress session and adoption of Swadeshi/Boycott/Swaraj/National Education as Congress creed
Deeper cause: clash between Moderate constitutionalism and Extremist mass mobilization philosophies
Outcome: Extremists expelled; Congress weakened organizationally for nearly a decade
UPSC trap: Surat Split is often confused as being about partition reversal — it was about methods, not goals

concepts.name: National Education Movement as a Pillar of Swadeshi
key_dimensions: Establishment of National Council of Education (1906) and Bengal National College — Aurobindo as first principal
Tagore's Shantiniketan as alternative educational philosophy rooted in indigenous culture
Distinction between boycott of government schools (political act) and building national schools (constructive act)
Connection to later Basic Education (Wardha Scheme) under Gandhi — continuity of thought

concepts.name: Indigenous Enterprise and Industrial Swadeshi
key_dimensions: Establishment of Swadeshi enterprises: Bengal Chemical (P.C. Ray), Bengal Pottery, National Textile mills
Role of Prafulla Chandra Ray as scientist-entrepreneur model linking science and nationalism
Limits of indigenous capital: lack of finance, skilled labor, and technology
UPSC trap: Swadeshi industrial enterprises largely failed economically but succeeded politically as symbols — distinction is important

concepts.name: Role of the Press and Literature in the Swadeshi Movement
key_dimensions: Newspapers: Yugantar, Kal (Tilak's Kesari in Marathi context), Sandhya (Brahmabandhab Upadhyay)
Sedition charges under Section 124A IPC — trials of Tilak, Upadhyay as landmark press freedom cases
Tagore's songs ('Amar Sonar Bangla' later became Bangladesh's national anthem) as cultural mobilization
UPSC trap: 'Amar Sonar Bangla' was written during Swadeshi (1905), not during Bangladesh liberation — chronology trap

concepts.name: Revolutionary Terrorism as a Radical Offshoot of the Swadeshi Movement
key_dimensions: Anushilan Samiti (Calcutta and Dhaka branches) and Jugantar — organizational structure of revolutionary nationalism
Alipore Bomb Case (1908) — Aurobindo Ghose's arrest and acquittal, his subsequent withdrawal from politics
Muzaffarpur bombing by Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki (1908) — intended target was Kingsford, but killed British women
UPSC trap: Revolutionary terrorism was inspired by but distinct from mainstream Swadeshi — leaders like Tilak inspired but did not endorse violence

concepts.name: Muslim Response to the Swadeshi Movement and Communal Fault Lines
key_dimensions: Nawab Salimullah of Dhaka's support for partition and founding of All India Muslim League (1906) — partition benefiting Muslim political identity
Reasons for limited Muslim participation in Swadeshi: economic interests in East Bengal, distrust of Hindu cultural symbols used in mobilization
Riots in East Bengal (1906-07) — communal violence as a tool to undermine Hindu-Muslim unity of Rakhi Bandhan
UPSC trap: Muslim League was founded in 1906 in Dhaka — direct political consequence of partition and Swadeshi — causal linkage often tested

concepts.name: Women's Participation in the Swadeshi Movement
key_dimensions: Breaking of purdah norms: women joining processions, picketing foreign cloth shops
Role of Sarala Devi Chaudhurani (Tagore's niece) in organizing Birshashthi festivals to glorify martial traditions
Distinction: women's participation was largely symbolic and upper-caste/class — not a mass women's movement
Comparison with Gandhi's mass inclusion of women in Civil Disobedience — Swadeshi as a precursor but limited

concepts.name: Annulment of Partition (1911) — Causes, Concession, and Consequences
key_dimensions: Announced at Delhi Durbar (December 1911) by King George V — partition reversed but Bengal reorganized on linguistic lines
British motives: administrative difficulties, rising revolutionary violence, WWI diplomatic considerations
Capital shifted from Calcutta to Delhi simultaneously — seen as punishment for Bengali nationalist militancy
UPSC trap: Reversal of partition is seen as a 'Moderate victory' but Extremists had weakened the movement by 1911 — credit attribution is a trap

concepts.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak's Role: Religious Mobilization and Swadeshi
key_dimensions: Ganesh Chaturthi and Shivaji festivals (pre-Swadeshi, 1893-95) as precedents for using religion in mass political mobilization
Tilak's formula: Swaraj is my birthright — linking Swadeshi to fundamental rights language
Tilak's sedition trial (1908) — sentenced to 6 years in Mandalay — galvanized public opinion
UPSC trap: Tilak used Hindu symbols but claimed they were cultural, not communal — distinction between cultural nationalism and religious communalism is frequently tested

concepts.name: Bipin Chandra Pal's Concept of 'New Nationalism' and Spiritual Nationalism
key_dimensions: Pal's argument that Swadeshi was not mere economic policy but a spiritual and civilizational assertion against Western materialism
His differences with Tilak: Pal was more pan-Indian and less rooted in Hindu revivalism
Pal's later disillusionment and political marginalization after Surat — a case study in extremist decline
Connection to Aurobindo's philosophical nationalism — overlaps and distinctions for comparative questions

concepts.name: Aurobindo Ghose: From Swadeshi Activist to Spiritual Nationalist
key_dimensions: His essay 'Doctrine of Passive Resistance' (1907) — systematic justification of boycott and passive resistance
Role as editor of Bande Mataram newspaper — sedition charges and acquittal
Alipore Case (1908-09) and spiritual transformation in jail — withdrawal from active politics to Pondicherry
UPSC trap: Aurobindo is sometimes clubbed with Extremists but his philosophical framework was distinct — passive resistance with potential for active resistance

concepts.name: Swadeshi and the Emergence of Mass Politics: Limits and Legacies
key_dimensions: Swadeshi as the first mass movement in Indian nationalism — but 'mass' was largely limited to Bengal's bhadralok (educated middle class)
Peasants and lower classes remained largely unmobilized — contrast with Gandhian mass movements
Legacy: established templates for boycott, national education, indigenous enterprise that Gandhi systematized later
UPSC trap: Swadeshi is called a 'mass movement' but historians like Sumit Sarkar distinguish it from truly mass participation — historiographical nuance

concepts.name: Bande Mataram: Song, Symbol, and Controversy
key_dimensions: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's Anandamath (1882) as source — original context of the novel (anti-Muslim undertones) vs. nationalist adoption
Adopted as the anthem of Swadeshi movement — 'Vande Mataram' chant as act of political defiance
Muslim objection to the song's religious imagery — Nehru Committee's 1937 compromise: only first two stanzas to be sung
UPSC trap: Bande Mataram was NOT India's national anthem — 'Jana Gana Mana' was chosen — reasons for the choice and the controversy are important

concepts.name: Swadeshi Movement and International Context: Irish, Russian, and Japanese Influences
key_dimensions: Irish Home Rule movement as a model for Indian passive resistance — Pal and Aurobindo explicitly cited Irish precedents
Japan's victory over Russia (1905) — psychological impact on Asian nationalism, proving Western powers were not invincible
Russian Revolution of 1905 — inspiration for mass strikes and general resistance
UPSC trap: These international influences are rarely asked directly but appear in sources/context questions in Mains — connecting global and Indian timelines

concepts.name: Government Repression and Legal Response to Swadeshi
key_dimensions: Seditious Meetings Act (1907) and Prevention of Seditious Meetings Act — legislative response to mass mobilization
Deportation of Lala Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh (1907) without trial — use of Regulation III of 1818
UPSC trap: Lajpat Rai was deported but NOT tried for sedition at this stage — distinction between administrative deportation and judicial trial
Pattern of repression: how government actions often escalated rather than suppressed movements — lesson applied in later nationalist strategy

concepts.name: Historiography of the Swadeshi Movement: Nationalist, Marxist, and Subaltern Perspectives
key_dimensions: Nationalist historiography (R.C. Majumdar): Swadeshi as heroic first mass assertion of national identity
Marxist historiography (Sumit Sarkar's 'The Swadeshi Movement in Bengal'): class character of the movement, bhadralok dominance, peasant exclusion
Subaltern Studies (Ranajit Guha, Partha Chatterjee): elite nationalist discourse vs. subaltern experience, failure to include peasants and workers
UPSC trap: Historiographical questions in Mains GS1 and optional History — ability to present multiple perspectives on the same event is a high-value skill
